question: What does the tachometer's green arc (1900 to 2550 RPM) represent, and where is the red line?

options.text: Normal operating range 1900-2550 RPM; red line (maximum) at 2550 RPM
Caution range 1900-2550 RPM; red line at 1900 RPM
Idle range only; no red line is marked
Normal operating range 1900-2550 RPM; red line (minimum) at 1900 RPM

explanation: The tachometer instrument markings show a normal operating range (green arc) of 1900 to 2550 RPM and a maximum (red line) of 2550 RPM.

question: What are the oil pressure gage's markings: minimum red line, green arc, and maximum red line?

options.text: Minimum 10 psi, green arc 30-50 psi, maximum 80 psi
Minimum 25 psi, green arc 60-90 psi, maximum 100 psi
Minimum 40 psi, green arc 60-90 psi, maximum 120 psi
Minimum 25 psi, green arc 40-60 psi, maximum 90 psi

explanation: Gage markings indicate minimum idling pressure of 25 PSI (red line), normal operating range of 60 to 90 PSI (green arc), and maximum pressure of 100 PSI (red line).

question: What are the oil temperature gage's normal operating range (green arc) and maximum (red line)?

options.text: Green arc 60°F-90°F, red line 100°F
Green arc 245°F-300°F, red line 350°F
Green arc 100°F-245°F, red line 245°F
Green arc 0°F-100°F, red line 245°F

explanation: Oil temperature limitations are the normal operating range (green arc) of 38°C (100°F) to 118°C (245°F), and a maximum (red line) of 118°C (245°F).

question: What is the desired suction range shown on the suction gage for proper operation of the attitude and directional indicators?

options.text: 1.0 to 2.0 inches of mercury
10 to 12 inches of mercury
6.0 to 8.0 inches of mercury
4.6 to 5.4 inches of mercury

explanation: The desired suction range on the suction gage is 4.6 to 5.4 inches of mercury; a reading below this range may indicate a malfunction, meaning the vacuum instruments should not be considered reliable.

question: What index marks appear on the attitude indicator's bank scale?

options.text: 10°, 20°, 30°, 60°, and 90° either side of the center mark
15°, 30°, 45°, and 60° either side only
5°, 10°, 15°, and 20° either side only
There are no index marks, only a horizon bar

explanation: Bank attitude is shown by a pointer relative to a bank scale with index marks at 10°, 20°, 30°, 60°, and 90° either side of the center mark.

question: Why must the directional indicator's compass card be reset periodically in flight?

options.text: It is affected by outside air temperature and must be recalibrated hourly
The directional indicator will precess slightly over time and must be re-adjusted to the magnetic compass
It resets itself automatically and never needs adjustment
It must be reset only after landing, never in flight

explanation: The directional indicator will precess slightly over a period of time, so the compass card should be set in accordance with the magnetic compass just prior to takeoff and occasionally re-adjusted on extended flights.

question: What supplies the suction necessary to operate the attitude and directional indicators?

options.text: An electric vacuum motor powered by the alternator
Ram air from the pitot tube
An engine-driven vacuum pump, with a vacuum relief valve and air filter behind the instrument panel
A hand-operated bellows pump

explanation: An engine-driven vacuum system provides the suction, consisting of a vacuum pump on the engine, a vacuum relief valve and air filter on the aft side of the firewall, and the instruments themselves.

question: What supplies ram air pressure and static pressure to the pitot-static instruments?

options.text: A single combined probe on the vertical stabilizer
The engine air induction system
The vacuum pump
A pitot tube on the lower left wing surface and an external static port on the lower left fuselage

explanation: The pitot-static system uses a pitot tube mounted on the lower surface of the left wing for ram air, and an external static port on the lower left side of the forward fuselage for static pressure.

question: Which instruments receive static pressure from the pitot-static system?

options.text: The airspeed indicator, rate-of-climb indicator, and altimeter
Only the altimeter
The tachometer and oil pressure gage
The attitude and directional indicators

explanation: Static pressure from the pitot-static system supplies the airspeed indicator, rate-of-climb indicator, and altimeter.

question: What circuit breaker amperage protects the heated pitot system, and what switch controls it?

options.text: A 5-amp breaker, controlled by a switch labeled HEAT
A 15-amp breaker, controlled by a rocker switch labeled PITOT HT
A 30-amp breaker, controlled by the master switch only
There is no circuit breaker for the pitot heat system

explanation: The heated pitot system uses a rocker-type switch labeled PITOT HT and is protected by a 15-amp circuit breaker under the engine controls on the instrument panel.

question: How is the true airspeed indicator's rotatable ring set to compute true airspeed?

options.text: By rotating the ring until it matches the tachometer RPM
By setting the ring to zero before every flight and never touching it again
By rotating the ring until pressure altitude is aligned with outside air temperature
By aligning the ring with the directional indicator's compass card

explanation: To operate the true airspeed indicator, the ring is rotated until pressure altitude is aligned with outside air temperature in degrees Fahrenheit, then true airspeed is read opposite the calibrated airspeed.

question: What operates the rate-of-climb indicator's pointer?

options.text: An electric motor driven from the alternator
Suction from the vacuum system
Direct linkage to the elevator trim wheel
Atmospheric pressure changes from altitude changes, supplied by the static source

explanation: The rate-of-climb indicator's pointer is actuated by atmospheric pressure changes resulting from altitude changes, as supplied by the static source.

question: How does the pilot adjust the altimeter for the current altimeter setting?

options.text: With a knob near the lower left portion of the indicator, adjusting the barometric scale
By recalibrating it against the suction gage
It has no adjustment; it is factory-set to sea level
By adjusting the directional indicator instead

explanation: A knob near the lower left portion of the altimeter provides adjustment of the barometric scale to the current altimeter setting.

question: How is pressure altitude obtained from the altimeter for use with the true airspeed ring?

options.text: By reading the altimeter with no adjustment at all
By momentarily setting the barometric scale to 29.92 and reading the altimeter, then resetting the original setting
By subtracting 1000 feet from indicated altitude
By using the rate-of-climb indicator instead

explanation: To obtain pressure altitude, the altimeter's barometric scale is momentarily set to 29.92, pressure altitude is read, and the original barometric setting is then restored.

question: What kind of stall warning system does the airplane use, and where is its inlet located?

options.text: An electric angle-of-attack vane on the fuselage nose
A pneumatic system with an inlet on the right wingtip
A pneumatic system with an inlet in the leading edge of the left wing
A stick-shaker mounted on the control column

explanation: The airplane uses a pneumatic-type stall warning system with an inlet in the leading edge of the left wing, an air-operated horn, and associated plumbing.

question: What physically causes the stall warning horn to sound as the airplane approaches a stall?

options.text: An electrical angle-of-attack sensor triggers a relay
The airspeed indicator directly drives the horn below a set speed
A mechanical linkage from the elevator trim wheel triggers the horn
Low pressure moving forward around the wing leading edge creates a differential pressure that draws air through the warning horn

explanation: As the airplane approaches a stall, low pressure on the upper wing surface moves forward around the leading edge, creating a differential pressure in the stall warning system that draws air through the warning horn.
